The Simplex turbopump is being developed at NASA/Marshall Space Flight Center by an in-house team.
The turbine has a total pressure of 800 psi at the inlet, a total-to-static pressure ratio of 15, and an inlet total temperature of 800°R.
The turbine is designed to supply 700 hp at a wheel speed of 25,000 rpm.
The initial bearing coolant circuit resulted in an unacceptable axial load of 15,000 lbf on the disk and a 15-point performance loss in turbine efficiency.
The optimized inducer design produced a non-cavitated total pressure rise of 197 psi with a net hydraulic efficiency of 73%.
The impeller generated a total pressure rise of 1,300 psi with a high predicted hydraulic efficiency of 95.6%.
The minimum inlet LOX pressure is 45 psi at 164°R flowing at 89.8 lbm/sec, yielding a required suction specific speed (Nss) of approximately 25,000 at the design point speed.
The initial 2D diffuser analysis showed separation on the pressure surface due to the impeller discharge flow angle of approximately 10°.
The modified diffuser design with a cutback on the leading edge of the vanes yielded a pressure rise of 288 psi.
The CFD analyses were used to verify one-dimensional predictions, assess aerodynamic and hydrodynamic designs, and provide flow environments for structural and thermal analyses.
The nozzle analysis was limited by size constraints that prevented resizing the nozzle to ensure isentropic flow.
The 2D rotor analysis did not fully capture the 3D effects of tip leakage.
The diffuser analysis required a 3D model to accurately capture the flow separation due to the impeller discharge angle.
The bearing coolant circuit was redesigned to reduce the axial load to 300 lbf and the performance loss to 0.001 lbm/sec of flow pulled from the hot gas path into the cavity.
The CFD analyses were used to optimize the inducer, impeller, and diffuser designs, as well as the bearing coolant circuit, to improve performance and reduce unacceptable loads and losses.
